content: The Commission on Accreditation of Medical Transport Systems (CAMTS) is an independent, non-profit organization that evaluates and accredits air and ground medical transport services in the United States. This includes both fixed-wing and rotary-wing air medical transport services, as well as ground-based inter-facility critical care transport services. CAMTS accreditation is based on a set of industry-established standards. As of June 2007, CAMTS had accredited 132 medical transport programs in the United States, along with three in Canada and one in South Africa. CAMTS first introduced its Accreditation Standards in 1991. These standards were developed collaboratively by its member organizations and through extensive public input. The standards emphasize that the primary focus of medical transport services should be on patient care and the safety of the transport environment. Accreditation by CAMTS is valid for three years, after which the program must undergo a re-audit to renew its accreditation. The initial accreditation process typically takes four to six months and involves a comprehensive review of all aspects of the organization’s operations, including management, medical protocols, and flight operations. CAMTS is composed of 14 member organizations, each of which has representation on its board of directors. These organizations include: Aerospace Medical Association Air Medical Physicians Association American Academy of Pediatrics American Association of Respiratory Care American College of Emergency Physicians Association of Air Medical Services National Air Transportation Association National Association of Air Medical Communications Specialists National Association of State EMS Directors National EMS Pilots Association National Flight Nurses Association National Flight Paramedics Association Although CAMTS accreditation is technically voluntary, many government jurisdictions require it as a condition for licensing medical transport services. This trend is growing as state health agencies address safety concerns related to emergency medical service flights. For example, states such as Colorado, New Jersey, New Mexico, Utah, and Washington mandate CAMTS accreditation for air ambulance services. Other states, such as Rhode Island and Texas, allow for either CAMTS accreditation or an equivalent process. Texas, for instance, has adopted CAMTS’ Accreditation Standards as its own and permits operators to undergo a state audit conducted by CAMTS-trained auditors if they choose not to pursue CAMTS accreditation. Similarly, Virginia and Oklahoma have incorporated CAMTS standards into their state licensing requirements. In 2003, CAMTS became involved in a legal dispute with Eagle Air Med, a medical transport provider operating in Utah. Eagle Air Med primarily served the Indian Health Service (IHS) on the Navajo Nation, which requires its contracted providers to hold CAMTS accreditation. During an application review, CAMTS discovered that Eagle Air Med had underreported its accident history, listing only one incident when there had actually been seven. Due to safety concerns, CAMTS had previously suspended Eagle Air Med’s accreditation twice. When CAMTS ultimately revoked the company’s accreditation in December 2002, Eagle Air Med filed a lawsuit and sought an injunction. In November 2003, a Utah district court ruled in favor of CAMTS, upholding the revocation of accreditation. However, the court allowed Eagle Air Med to reapply for accreditation after six months. Several notable medical transport programs have achieved CAMTS accreditation, including: Air Evac ARCH Air Medical Service Lifestar Air Medical Services Memorial Hermann Life Flight STAT Medevac
